item.content:encoded:
Okay, I think I have a reason of why this actually worked better than with a streamlined tale.

Spoilers ahead
Even though it's just my take to the whole thing

To put it simply. This is a take on what the hell happens right after you get caught by a Berryman-Langford memetic kill agent when you've no clearance, right? And what is the most eye-catching elements in those?

Fractals and Spirals. This the reason this partly works as a CYOA.

You see, I was "lucky" to get the Berryman-Langford reference as my second ending (first one obviously the "take it" end route). Thanks to that I got all the way back and saw it from a new perspective. Imagine trying to write a narrative representation of a BL kill meme; basically, how the mind of the victim is forced to work from the moment of exposure onwards. Fractals and spirals are coming out for sure. And how would you represent those in a narrative setting? I'd probably choose repetition and scalation, which is exactly what this proposal is completely filled with.

For that reason, the CYOA format is not there to give you or the main character any choice besides a dreadful end but to let you run through the exact nature of what the meme is all about.

Fractals and Spirals. I don't know how to scalate this even further, sorry.

PS: I know there's that end in which Petroskey probably lived out the BL killmeme ("take the easy way out" end route), but that one is the most dreadful one in-universe. Long story short, the Foundation as a whole is having one really bad week after that.

item.content:encoded:
A very interesting article indeed. The writing was great. It went far beyond any cheap attempt at over-descriptiveness. I feel like some of it had the surreal, somewhat comical tone of Terry Pratchet (the mountain of Morgan and Grauer, things like that). The multiple choice thing was interesting, but in the end there were only 3 endings. I'm not sure I fully grasp the meaning, though I do find it interesting.

SPOILERS SINCE I CAN'T FIGURE OUT COLLAPSIBLES APPARENTLY

+ Show Block
- Close

In the end, I'm pretty sure the memetic kill agent was the cause of all this. And he thought the security breach was the failing of the kill agent. I guess, in the end, this is about a meaningless existence that wants to make things more exciting, only to become trapped in a meaningless reality. Interesting how the main character started reinventing himself for one option. It just didn't work. The best ending, I guess, is the one where he goes back to his boring life. The only ending where anything truly meaningful (at least in the eyes of the main character) happens leaves him still there. Of course he didn't actually push away all the illusions. He just created a new one for himself. Not sure what the message is in that, I think the endings where he's back at his cubicle are indeed reality. Why would he imagine bleeding so much and dying once?
Thing is, I think I've got the message, but maybe it wasn't really emphasized enough. Maybe it's not a message. Maybe it's just a tragic story. Definitely it was a worthwhile experience.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Most of this makes sense, but I have a few clarifications I want to respond with.

Responses
– hide block

While I do partly agree that calling it a CYOA brings certain expectations along with it, I think that by offering the reader choices, you're implying that the reader's choices are supposed to be important. There was this inherent sense of self-involvement. The reader has to click the button to go to the next page. The reader has to make the choice. It's not like the words just keep going, but essentially the reader has to consciously advance the story of their own volition. That in and of itself conflicts with the way that the story happens to emmet instead of being driven by Emmet. Like, I get that wasn't your intention, but in my opinion, its almost unavoidable when you're asking the reader to click through it themselves.

Your second point is a fair one, and honestly I haven't tried writing in second person in a skip so I'm not well acquainted with the problems you have to overcome with that.

As for your third point, you do definitely answer the questions, but the narrative is not written as like… an active search to find out the answer to the first question. I think I would've been more driven by the second question if I had more an opportunity to get characterization for the protag, or maybe if I had some idea in my head what was going to happen to the protagonist, but since I didn't like… I didn't have enough time to feel attached to the main character before I was expected to start caring about him. I think more time getting to know our protag before diving deep into the existential aspect of the piece would've benefitted (although I admit I have no good idea on how you really make that work, since the logical flow mandates you jump straight to the interrogation)

As for your third point, I understand that as a concern, but I know enough people who came out of this closer to confused and "oh I get it" that I think it was a miscalculation on your part. It's a reasonable miscalculation, and what you have is like… like it obviously works. I just feel like, even if you might've beaten some of your readers over the head, a switch to a visual form of storytelling from this heavily textual one you've gone with would've been a rewarding experience even for people who figured it out before the ending.

Again, I understand that like, there's nothing you really could do at this point. I appreciate you taking the time to type out responses, so yeah. Cheers!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm sorry the story didn't do much for you. I doubt anything I could say about it after the fact could make you enjoy it more (or less), but I do appreciate getting such extensive feedback. I'll do my best to respond, if only to give an explanation of why it's taken the form it has.

There's definitely spoilers here too.
There's definitely spoilers here too.

Regarding the format: I think expectations have certainly been affected by the term 'choose your own adventure.' I didn't set out to write something where the player has a huge amount of agency on the macro-level, and as you identified, the character himself has a very small amount of power in shaping their fate. I think something like 'branch-based storytelling' would be a more apt descriptor. In my opinion, each path should be taken as part of a whole.

Secondarily, I chose to format things this way precisely because it removes the reader from the context of the wiki. I did the same in 910 for that reason. In my own experimentation, I didn't find that a shift to second person while surrounded by the trappings of the main site worked at all. Experiences will differ, but it was a considered choice. Twine also made it much easier for me to make changes in blocks of text as they're seen multiple times, and also removes the context of seeing what comes immediately before and after any given portion. I think this is an important factor in creating a disorienting experience. Also, I just wanted to make something with Twine again.

Regarding a central question: I think the most pertinent questions here are 'what's going on?' and 'what will happen to the central character?' I think I answer both of these fairly clearly upon a thorough reading of the piece, though I'm open to changes if that's not the case. Questions about SCP-001 itself are answered on the first page. There's no data about it there. Maybe there never has been. The title of the piece is relevant here.

Regarding inclusion of a kill agent: I hadn't thought of including the image, but I think it would be beating the reader over the head a little. It's not an image that's itself particularly scary or startling (at least in my eyes,) so I'd be more worried about readers going "yeah, I got that already." I might be wrong about the strength of an ending like that, but changing things would require more rewriting than I really want to do right now regardless.

I hope that gives you some additional sense of closure about the piece.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This story bothers me. Like, deeply bothers me. Because like, this idea, this concept, and even the prose, is fantastic. It is clever as fuck and I have to respect that. But somehow, this execution did nothing for me. I've been trying to pin down why this doesn't do anything for me, and honestly it seems like its doing well for everyone else, so its not like my words here will carry a ton of weight.

Long Rant Incoming, and Spoilers I Guess
– hide block

So, the core conceit of this is brilliant. Writing an 001 about the kill agent is amazing. But between making this a CYOA, and just your pacing choices bring me out of the story before I really hit the hard ending and have any sense of "a-ha".

Let's talk about the choice to make this a CYOA. The very first thing that this does to me is that it's already fighting my sense of immersion, because I'm taken away from the site, and I'm asked to essentially click through second person narration. Also, given the narrative that you've opted for (one based around the idea of essentially waiting around for death to come and take you), I never really felt any agency while clicking through it. It's fairly obvious from the tone you strike and the nature of being shoved into a room that I'm not really gong to ultimately affect the outcome, and since I have no clear goal, any sense of "let me try to accomplish this" is lost. So, by making this a CYOA, you've introduced a narrative style and gimmick that kind of contradicts the tone and narrative you're telling, since there's not really anything the reader can do.

Also, from just the way the narrative is laid out, most of the story happens to our protagonist, instead of being driven forward by the character's actions. Sure, we have choices in the road, but it never really feels like we're in control of our own situation. This results in another strike against the CYOA execution, since it felt like kind of a drag to sit through the story happening to me instead of feeling a sense of controlling the outcome.

Now I want to talk about the actual narrative itself, outside of the CYOA context. The way that this is written, it takes it sweet time with doing much. You have two sequences that consist of repeating the same situation (even though you get different dialogue options, for pacing purposes this still feels somewhat repetitive). All in all this makes for a slow and poignant read, which isn't a bad thing in and of itself! Slow can be used really nicely, usually in contrast with faster paced sections, or possibly to build dread. However, here the slowness makes me wish I could get to the point faster. Since you're not entirely forthcoming with what is going on, you're effectively building a mystery. However, there's no clear question I felt like I was trying to answer. I guess there was the general question of "what is going on?", but the way the narrative grounds itself in the action that is happening in any given scene, it doesn't feel like I'm making strides toward answering really any question. The lack of clear question or like, end goal makes the slow pacing feel like a drag instead of building tension. You don't have to give us the answer, but you should have made the question more clear, in my opinion.

I guess you could argue that the question is "what was SCP-001?", but the narrative does not present that as the conflict. The conflict is more between Emmet and their captors, and doesn't focus a ton on what SCP-001 actually is, instead delving into the things Emmet tries to do to get out of their situation, but since the tone of the piece and options we're given as part of the CYOA imply that we're not going to escape, the end of this conflict felt like a foregone conclusion.

Now, honestly I think that the idea of using this slow, defeated tone isn't a bad idea in and of itself. However, I feel like pairing this with your core conflict and the CYOA style is not doing yourself any favors. I think you could've written the same style of tone in a slightly more stream-of-conscious manner, without the CYOA component and possibly gotten a much better reaction.

Finally, my biggest peeve with this is one major opportunity that it missed. I don't know how you fix it, or how you even structure the article so this works, but I am convinced it can be done:

You didn't use the actual kill agent as the stinger.

The memetic kill agent is an inherently visual thing. It is distinct, and everyone knows what it is when they see it. You do some clever hinting and its more subtle, and that's a fine stylistic choice but like… realizing that the entire time this was caused by the memetic kill agent would be such a more rewarding realization if the final clue was just an image. No words even needed. You could just stick the image after you say he dies. Honestly, if you managed to end this with a picture of the kill agent in its current form, that might've gotten me to upvote in spite of all of my previous complaints, because such a visual stinger like that is using this format, and the site's lore, to the best you can. An SCP is as much a visual story telling medium as a textual one. I feel like this article should've taken more advantage of that, especially since it is about one of the most famous pictures on the site.

Ok, that's all. This article has been bothering me a lot because I felt like it should've done something for me. Now I've finally been able to articulate why it hasn't done anything for me, and what I personally would've tried to do to get it to do something for me. Like, the idea is fantastic, and your grasp of prose is excellent, but the overall product just did not come together for me.

But I guess you did manage to evoke this reaction from me, and that's gotta count for something, right? :P

It's mildly obfuscated by the mild format screw, but that's entirely justified by the nature of SCP-001.
